title: Metric staleness detection and trace anchor strategy
content:
Summary:

This note proposes a lightweight, low-query-cost approach to detect metric staleness across our inference stacks and to use tracing anchors to make staleness investigations fast and deterministic. Focus is on per-tenant and per-route signal freshness for token-serving metrics (latency_p50/p95, token_count, kv_cache_hit_rate) and on designing small, actionable dashboard widgets and alerts that minimize query cost and false positives.

Motivation / problem statement (short):
- We sometimes see dashboards go quiet (flatlines) after infra changes, exporter restarts, or when ingestion pipelines drop events.
- Existing alerts are noisy (either alert on expected low-volume tenants or miss slow-developing ingestion problems).
- Investigations take too long because traces aren't anchored to the metric ingestion timeline; we have to stitch traces post-hoc.

Goals:
- Detect staleness quickly with a few cheap checks per minute per logical scope (global, region, model-route, tenant).
- Provide trace anchors (a tiny trace event inserted at metric ingestion) so a single click jumps to representative traces from the stale window.
- Make dashboard widgets resilient: show freshness, last-ingest age, and a compact heatmap of recent heartbeat success.

Definitions and heuristics:
- Freshness window: the expected frequency of metric emission for a scope. Defaults: global: 10s, route-level: 60s, tenant-level high-traffic: 10s, tenant-level low-traffic: 5m.
- Staleness: no metric datapoint received for > 3x freshness window. Use exponential backoff thresholds for low-volume scopes to avoid noise.
- Partial staleness: some metrics for scope present (eg token_count) but mission-critical metrics missing (latency_p95). Flag as partial.

Detection algorithm (cheap, approximate):
1) Heartbeat counter incremented by exporter: hb_count per scope every emission.
2) In the metrics store (long-retention aggregator) run an inexpensive count-over-time check: queries that only touch rollup tables or pre-computed counters.
3) Evaluate three derived flags:
   - missing_all (no heartbeat samples in last 3x window)
   - missing_key_metrics (heartbeat present but x% of key metrics missing for last window)
   - reduced_cardinality (number of unique hosts/exporters for scope drops suddenly)
4) Alert if missing_all == true OR (missing_key_metrics == true AND reduced_cardinality == true).

Example (pseudo-SQL) for route-level missing_all check (use rollup table 'metric_rollups'):

SELECT
  route_id,
  max(ts) as last_seen_ts,
  now() - max(ts) as age_seconds
FROM metric_rollups
WHERE metric_name = 'hb_count'
  AND route_id = 'text-generation/v1'
  AND ts >= now() - interval '1 day'
GROUP BY route_id
HAVING now() - max(ts) > interval '180 seconds';

Notes on query cost: use rollup tables that are updated every 10s–60s; avoid raw-event scans. Rollups should include max(ts) and count in last window.

Trace anchoring strategy:
- When the metric exporter emits a rollout/heartbeat, also emit a tiny tracing span (trace anchor) with a standardized tag: anchor.scope=<scope>, anchor.type=metric-hb, anchor.ts=<ingest-ts>.
- Tracing span should be extremely cheap, sampled at 1% by default for global scope and 10% for high-priority tenants. But the span must always be emitted (sampler decision can be low-cost) and flagged with a separate index in trace storage so it can be queried independently of sampled spans.
- The span body/payload: minimal: scope id, exporter id, emission id (uuid), timestamp. No large payloads.
- Store an inverted index mapping anchor.emission_id -> trace_id so that, when we detect staleness, we can query recent anchors for that scope and surface sample traces that were active around the failure window.

Sampling and fallback rules:
- If the application-level trace sampler rejects a span, still write the anchor marker to the anchor index (separate lightweight RPC) to guarantee visibility; avoid full trace storage costs.
- On large-scale incidents we can bump anchor sampling to 100% for the affected region via config or a rollout flag.

Dashboard UI/Widgets (compact, cheap):
- Freshness badge (small pill widget): shows last-ingest age for selected scope with color thresholds: green < 1x window, yellow 1–3x, red > 3x. Clicking shows top 3 recent anchors with link to traces.
- Heatline (sparkline with gaps): renders hb_count time series with gaps. Implement client-side gap detection; gray out missing segments rather than extrapolating.
- Partial-staleness indicator: a stacked bar showing which key metrics are missing (latency, tokens, cache_rate).
- Cost-aware rollup selector: default dashboard queries should use rollups; allow a toggle "drill to raw" which will run the heavier queries only on user action.

Alerting and runbook (short):
- Primary symptom: Freshness badge turns red for route X.
- Quick triage steps: 1) check exporter host count (reduced_cardinality) 2) list recent anchors for the scope (last 15m) -> if anchors exist, pick one and open trace 3) check exporter logs (link to central log index) 4) validate config push or deployment events in the last hour (links to CI/CD job ids).
- Escalation: if missing_all persists for > 10 minutes for a route with SLA-backed customers, page oncall SRE and notify product owner.

Investigation tips / heuristics for false positives: 
- Low-volume tenants often show long gaps by design — use tenant-level dynamic freshness windows based on historical emission rate (p50 inter-arrival).
- If hb_count present but latency_p95 missing, check metric collector config for the histogram/percentile export path — histograms sometimes drop if bucketization changes.

Implementation checklist (MVP):
- [ ] Add hb_count emitter to lightweight exporter (PR + tests)
- [ ] Add anchor span emission and minimal anchor index (backend PR + migration)
- [ ] Add rollup hooks: max(ts), count_last_window, unique_host_count
- [ ] Dashboard components: freshness badge + heatline + partial indicator
- [ ] Alert rules: missing_all and combined partial+cardinality
- [ ] Runbook doc and Slack/PagerDuty routing

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Where to store the anchor index? Options: separate low-cost time-series DB vs tagging in trace storage. Trade-off between query cost and store duplication.
- Sampling policy: default sampler percentages may need tuning per region and per-customer SLA.
- UX: how aggressively should dashboards hide noisy low-volume scopes? Prefer default hide + user opt-in.

Next steps / owners (proposal):
- Priya: owner for metric schema + rollup integration (2 weeks)
- Evan: anchor index prototype + backend storage options (2 weeks)
- Marta: dashboard component and alert rule templates (1.5 weeks)
- Follow-up meeting: schedule 2025-03-06 to review prototype metrics and anchor demo.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could piggyback anchor writes onto the same path as logging light-weight signals (kafka topic 'anchors') so they are cheap to consume and index.
- Consider a "staleness confidence score" combining age, host_count_drop, and key_metric_ratio so alerts can be prioritized.

- Quick rollup query examples (internal): CONFLUENCE-OBS-STALENESS-123
- Instrumentation PR: https://github.com/redwood/instrumentation/pull/89
